claim: Submovements during continuous tracking movements occur 2-3 times per second.
source: Using spatiotemporal perturbations in humans, we demonstrate that apparently discrete submovements made 2–3 times per second reflect constructive interference between motor errors and continuous feedback corrections that are filtered by intrinsic circuitry in the motor system.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Submovements reflect constructive interference between motor errors and continuous feedback corrections that are filtered by intrinsic circuitry in the motor system.
source: Using spatiotemporal perturbations in humans, we demonstrate that apparently discrete submovements made 2–3 times per second reflect constructive interference between motor errors and continuous feedback corrections that are filtered by intrinsic circuitry in the motor system.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from spatiotemporal perturbations.

claim: Local field potentials in monkey motor cortex revealed characteristic signatures of a Kalman filter.
source: Local field potentials in monkey motor cortex revealed characteristic signatures of a Kalman filter, giving rise to both low-frequency cortical cycles during movement, and delta oscillations during sleep.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from LFP recordings in monkeys.

claim: Kalman filter signatures in motor cortex give rise to both low-frequency cortical cycles during movement and delta oscillations during sleep.
source: Local field potentials in monkey motor cortex revealed characteristic signatures of a Kalman filter, giving rise to both low-frequency cortical cycles during movement, and delta oscillations during sleep.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: The intrinsic rhythmicity of motor cortical networks reflects an internal model of external dynamics used for state estimation during feedback-guided movement.
source: We interpret these results within the framework of optimal feedback control, and suggest that the intrinsic rhythmicity of motor cortical networks reflects an internal model of external dynamics, which is used for state estimation during feedback-guided movement.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation stated in the abstract.

claim: Movement intermittency was first described over a century ago.
source: Although first described over a century ago (Woodworth, 1899; Craik, 1947; Vince, 1948) the cause of movement intermittency remains debated.
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical work.

claim: The cause of movement intermittency remains debated.
source: Although first described over a century ago (Woodworth, 1899; Craik, 1947; Vince, 1948) the cause of movement intermittency remains debated.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Submovements often disappear in the absence of vision.
source: Submovements often disappear in the absence of vision (Miall et al., 1993a) and are influenced by feedback delays (Miall, 1996), suggesting that their timing depends on extrinsic properties of visuomotor feedback loops.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Submovements are influenced by feedback delays.
source: Submovements often disappear in the absence of vision (Miall et al., 1993a) and are influenced by feedback delays (Miall, 1996), suggesting that their timing depends on extrinsic properties of visuomotor feedback loops.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Submovement timing depends on extrinsic properties of visuomotor feedback loops.
source: Submovements often disappear in the absence of vision (Miall et al., 1993a) and are influenced by feedback delays (Miall, 1996), suggesting that their timing depends on extrinsic properties of visuomotor feedback loops.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited evidence about vision and feedback delays.

claim: Some rhythmicity persists in the absence of feedback.
source: However, some rhythmicity persists in the absence of feedback (Doeringer and Hogan, 1998), and it has been suggested that an internal refractory period, clock or oscillator parses complex movements into discrete, isochronal segments (Viviani and Flash, 1995; Loram et al., 2006; Hogan and Sternad, 2012; Russell and Sternad, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: An internal refractory period, clock or oscillator parses complex movements into discrete, isochronal segments.
source: However, some rhythmicity persists in the absence of feedback (Doeringer and Hogan, 1998), and it has been suggested that an internal refractory period, clock or oscillator parses complex movements into discrete, isochronal segments (Viviani and Flash, 1995; Loram et al., 2006; Hogan and Sternad, 2012; Russell and Sternad, 2001).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Cyclical dynamics within motor cortical networks have a time period of 300-500 ms.
source: Cyclical dynamics within motor cortical networks with a time period of 300–500 ms may reflect the neural correlates of such an intrinsic oscillator (Churchland et al., 2012; Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cyclical dynamics in motor cortical networks may reflect the neural correlates of an intrinsic oscillator.
source: Cyclical dynamics within motor cortical networks with a time period of 300–500 ms may reflect the neural correlates of such an intrinsic oscillator (Churchland et al., 2012; Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of cited findings.

claim: During continuous tracking, each submovement is phase-locked to a single cortical cycle.
source: During continuous tracking, each submovement is phase-locked to a single cortical cycle, giving rise to low-frequency coherence between cortical oscillations and movement speed (Jerbi et al., 2007; Hall et al., 2014; Pereira et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phase-locking between submovements and cortical cycles gives rise to low-frequency coherence between cortical oscillations and movement speed.
source: During continuous tracking, each submovement is phase-locked to a single cortical cycle, giving rise to low-frequency coherence between cortical oscillations and movement speed (Jerbi et al., 2007; Hall et al., 2014; Pereira et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Intrinsic dynamics of recurrently-connected cortical networks act as an 'engine of movement' responsible for internal generation and timing of the descending motor command.
source: It has been proposed that the intrinsic dynamics of recurrently-connected cortical networks act as an 'engine of movement', responsible for internal generation and timing of the descending motor command (Churchland et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Low-frequency dynamics observed in motor cortex may arise from sensorimotor feedback loops through the external environment.
source: However, another possibility is that low-frequency dynamics observed in motor cortex arise from sensorimotor feedback loops through the external environment.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Cortical cycles appear conserved across a wide range of behaviors and share a common structure with delta oscillations during sleep.
source: On the one hand, cortical cycles appear conserved across a wide range of behaviors and even share a common structure with delta oscillations during sleep (Hall et al., 2014), consistent with a purely intrinsic origin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The conservation of cortical cycles across behaviors and sleep is consistent with a purely intrinsic origin.
source: On the one hand, cortical cycles appear conserved across a wide range of behaviors and even share a common structure with delta oscillations during sleep (Hall et al., 2014), consistent with a purely intrinsic origin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited evidence.

claim: The influence of feedback delays on submovement timing suggests an extrinsic contribution to movement intermittency.
source: On the other hand, the influence of feedback delays on submovement timing suggests an extrinsic contribution to movement intermittency.
evidence: This is an inference from previously cited evidence about feedback delays.

claim: Under unperturbed feedback conditions, power spectra of cursor angular velocity generally exhibited a principal peak at around 2 Hz.
source: Under unperturbed feedback conditions, power spectra generally exhibited a principal peak at around 2 Hz (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Submovement frequency was only slightly affected by target speed.
source: This frequency was only slightly affected by target speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports (Miall, 1996) and perhaps suggestive of an intrinsic oscillator or clock determining submovement timing.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: The slight effect of target speed on submovement frequency is consistent with previous reports.
source: This frequency was only slightly affected by target speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports (Miall, 1996) and perhaps suggestive of an intrinsic oscillator or clock determining submovement timing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The slight effect of target speed on submovement frequency is suggestive of an intrinsic oscillator or clock determining submovement timing.
source: This frequency was only slightly affected by target speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports (Miall, 1996) and perhaps suggestive of an intrinsic oscillator or clock determining submovement timing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: With a feedback delay of 100 ms, the frequency of the primary submovement peak reduced to around 1.4 Hz.
source: With delays of 100 and 200 ms, the frequency of the primary peak reduced to around 1.4 and 1 Hz respectively (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2), demonstrating that submovement timing in fact depended on extrinsic feedback properties.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: With a feedback delay of 200 ms, the frequency of the primary submovement peak reduced to around 1 Hz.
source: With delays of 100 and 200 ms, the frequency of the primary peak reduced to around 1.4 and 1 Hz respectively (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2), demonstrating that submovement timing in fact depended on extrinsic feedback properties.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The reduction in submovement frequency with feedback delays demonstrates that submovement timing depends on extrinsic feedback properties.
source: With delays of 100 and 200 ms, the frequency of the primary peak reduced to around 1.4 and 1 Hz respectively (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2), demonstrating that submovement timing in fact depended on extrinsic feedback properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: With increased delays, a further peak appeared at approximately three times the frequency of the primary peak.
source: Interestingly, a further peak appeared at approximately three times the frequency of the primary peak, and with increased delays, of 300 and 400 ms, a fifth harmonic was observed.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: With delays of 300 and 400 ms, a fifth harmonic was observed in the velocity spectrum.
source: Interestingly, a further peak appeared at approximately three times the frequency of the primary peak, and with increased delays, of 300 and 400 ms, a fifth harmonic was observed.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The time-periods of the first, third and fifth harmonics were linearly related to extrinsic delay times, with gradients of 1.89 ± 0.20, 0.59 ± 0.04 and 0.33 ± 0.11 respectively.
source: The time-periods of the first, third and fifth harmonics were linearly related to extrinsic delay times, with gradients of 1.89 ± 0.20, 0.59 ± 0.04 and 0.33 ± 0.11 respectively (Figure 1E, Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from regression analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Subtracting a delayed version from the original signal is known as comb filtering.
source: In signal-processing terms, subtracting a delayed version from the original signal is known as comb filtering (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is established knowledge from signal processing.

claim: Intermittency arises as a byproduct of continuous, linear feedback control with inherent time delays.
source: According to this extrinsic interpretation, intermittency arises not from active internal generation of discrete submovement events, but as a byproduct of continuous, linear feedback control with inherent time delays.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: Submovement frequencies reflect components of broad-band motor noise that are exacerbated by constructive interference with delayed feedback corrections.
source: Instead these frequencies reflect components of broad-band motor noise that are exacerbated by constructive interference with delayed feedback corrections.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: Artificial errors at submovement frequencies would be harder to track than perturbations at frequencies absent from the velocity spectrum.
source: Our hypothesis was that artificial errors at submovement frequencies would be harder to track (because of constructive interference) than perturbations at frequencies absent from the velocity spectrum.
evidence: This is the hypothesis tested in the second experiment.

claim: With a 2 Hz perturbation and no feedback delay, the peak angular velocity of force responses occurred around the same time as the peak angular velocity of the perturbation.
source: Figure 2A shows example tracking behavior with a 2 Hz perturbation. Note that the peak angular velocity of force responses (black line, calculated from the subject's finger forces) occurred around the same time as the peak angular velocity of the perturbation (green line).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: With a 2 Hz perturbation and no feedback delay, the angular velocity of the cursor exhibited pronounced oscillations that were larger than the perturbation.
source: As a result, the angular velocity of the cursor (yellow line, reflecting the combination of the subject's forces with the perturbation) exhibited pronounced oscillations that were larger than the perturbation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: With a 2 Hz perturbation and 200 ms feedback delay, peaks in force velocity coincided with perturbation troughs, attenuating the disturbance to cursor velocity.
source: Figure 2B shows performance in the same task when visual feedback was delayed by 200 ms. In this condition, peaks in force velocity coincided with perturbation troughs, attenuating the disturbance to cursor velocity.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: With no feedback delay, perturbations at 2 Hz induced a large peak in the cursor velocity spectrum, indicating that the artificial error was not effectively tracked.
source: As previously, in the absence of feedback delay, the frequency of submovements was around 2 Hz. Correspondingly, perturbations at 2 Hz induced a large peak in the cursor velocity spectrum, indicating that the artificial error was not effectively tracked.
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: With a feedback delay of 200 ms, the cursor velocity spectrum with a 2 Hz perturbation was attenuated.
source: By contrast, with a feedback delay of 200 ms the cursor velocity spectrum with a 2 Hz perturbation was attenuated.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: With a feedback delay of 200 ms, the largest spectral peaks were associated with 1 and 3 Hz perturbations, matching the frequencies of submovements in this delay condition.
source: The largest spectral peaks were instead associated with 1 and 3 Hz perturbations, matching the frequencies of submovements in this delay condition.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cursor amplitude responses greater than unity at 2 Hz (with no delay), and at 1 and 3 Hz (with 200 ms delay) indicate exacerbation of intermittencies introduced by artificial errors at submovement frequencies.
source: Cursor amplitude responses greater than unity at 2 Hz (with no delay), and at 1 and 3 Hz (with 200 ms delay) indicate exacerbation of intermittencies introduced by artificial errors at submovement frequencies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ANOVA revealed a highly significant interaction between delay time and perturbation frequency on cursor amplitude response (n = 8 subjects, F4,70=110.2, p<0.0001).
source: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) with two factors (delay time and perturbation frequency) revealed a highly significant interaction (n = 8 subjects, F4,70=110.2, p<0.0001), confirming the interdependence of feedback delays and frequencies of constructive/destructive interference.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: The significant interaction between delay time and perturbation frequency confirms the interdependence of feedback delays and frequencies of constructive/destructive interference.
source: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) with two factors (delay time and perturbation frequency) revealed a highly significant interaction (n = 8 subjects, F4,70=110.2, p<0.0001), confirming the interdependence of feedback delays and frequencies of constructive/destructive interference.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical result.

claim: Force amplitude responses were largely independent of extrinsic delay.
source: Unlike the cursor amplitude responses described previously, force amplitude responses were largely independent of extrinsic delay.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Feedback gains were attenuated at higher frequencies.
source: However, as with the velocity spectra in Figure 1D, feedback gains were also attenuated at higher frequencies.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Two-factor ANOVA confirmed a significant main effect of frequency on force amplitude response (n = 8 subjects, F4,70=36.3, p<0.0001).
source: A two-factor ANOVA confirmed a significant main effect of frequency (n = 8 subjects, F4,70=36.3, p<0.0001) but not delay time (F1,70=3.1, p=0.08), and only a weakly significant interaction (F4,70=2.9, p=0.03).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Two-factor ANOVA found no significant main effect of delay time on force amplitude response (F1,70=3.1, p=0.08).
source: A two-factor ANOVA confirmed a significant main effect of frequency (n = 8 subjects, F4,70=36.3, p<0.0001) but not delay time (F1,70=3.1, p=0.08), and only a weakly significant interaction (F4,70=2.9, p=0.03).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Two-factor ANOVA found only a weakly significant interaction between frequency and delay time on force amplitude response (F4,70=2.9, p=0.03).
source: A two-factor ANOVA confirmed a significant main effect of frequency (n = 8 subjects, F4,70=36.3, p<0.0001) but not delay time (F1,70=3.1, p=0.08), and only a weakly significant interaction (F4,70=2.9, p=0.03).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Feedback corrections to artificial errors revealed a delay-independent filter matching the attenuation of submovement peaks at higher frequencies.
source: In other words, feedback corrections to artificial errors revealed a delay-independent filter matching the attenuation of submovement peaks at higher frequencies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the force amplitude response data.

claim: The phase delay of force responses was influenced by perturbation frequency.
source: Interestingly, the phase delay of force responses was also influenced by perturbation frequency (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Corrections to low-frequency perturbations occurred slightly earlier than those to higher frequencies, indicating a predictive component to feedback responses.
source: Effectively, corrections to low-frequency perturbations occurred slightly earlier than those to higher frequencies, indicating a predictive component to feedback responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phase delay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: There was a significant effect of frequency on phase delay of force responses (F4,70=9.5, p<0.0001).
source: As with the amplitude response, there was a significant effect of frequency (F4,70=9.5, p<0.0001) but not extrinsic delay (F1,70 =2.6, p=0.12) on this phase delay, and no significant interaction (F4,70=0.7, p=0.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant effect of extrinsic delay on phase delay of force responses (F1,70=2.6, p=0.12).
source: As with the amplitude response, there was a significant effect of frequency (F4,70=9.5, p<0.0001) but not extrinsic delay (F1,70 =2.6, p=0.12) on this phase delay, and no significant interaction (F4,70=0.7, p=0.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant interaction between frequency and extrinsic delay on phase delay of force responses (F4,70=0.7, p=0.6).
source: As with the amplitude response, there was a significant effect of frequency (F4,70=9.5, p<0.0001) but not extrinsic delay (F1,70 =2.6, p=0.12) on this phase delay, and no significant interaction (F4,70=0.7, p=0.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: The frequencies of feedforward movements can readily exceed submovement frequencies observed during feedback-guided behavior.
source: However, it is well-known that the frequencies of feedforward movements can readily exceed submovement frequencies observed during feedback-guided behavior (Kunesch et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Subjects could generate force fluctuations up to 5 Hz with little attenuation in the feedforward task.
source: In this case, subjects could generate force fluctuations up to 5 Hz with little attenuation (Figure 2J,K and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the feedforward task data.

claim: Filtering of corrective responses is not an inherent property of feedforward motor pathways but instead reflects intrinsic dynamics in the visuomotor feedback loop.
source: Therefore we concluded that filtering of corrective responses was not an inherent property of feedforward motor pathways but instead reflected intrinsic dynamics in the visuomotor feedback loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing feedback and feedforward task data.

claim: Discrepancies while tracking slowly-moving objects in the physical world are unlikely to change quickly.
source: However, while feedforward movements can in some cases approach these frequencies, discrepancies while tracking slowly-moving objects in the physical world are unlikely to change quickly.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the physical constraints of tracking tasks.

claim: Limbs and real-world targets will tend to move with a constant velocity unless acted upon by a force.
source: The limbs and real-world targets will tend (to a first approximation) to move with a constant velocity unless acted upon by a force.
evidence: This is an application of Newtonian physics to the tracking task.

claim: The drift in force production during isometric tasks is dominated by low-frequency components.
source: Moreover, even for isometric tasks, the drift in force production is dominated by low-frequency components (Baweja et al., 2009; Slifkin and Newell, 2000), possibly consistent with neural integration in the descending motor pathway (Shadmehr, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Low-frequency drift in force production is possibly consistent with neural integration in the descending motor pathway.
source: Moreover, even for isometric tasks, the drift in force production is dominated by low-frequency components (Baweja et al., 2009; Slifkin and Newell, 2000), possibly consistent with neural integration in the descending motor pathway (Shadmehr, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: An optimal state estimator should attribute high-frequency errors to sensory noise.
source: Given inherent uncertainties in sensation, an optimal state estimator should attribute high-frequency errors to sensory noise (which is unconstrained by Newtonian and/or neuromuscular dynamics).
evidence: This is an inference based on optimal control theory.

claim: A Kalman filter continuously integrates new evidence with updated estimates of the current state, evolving according to a model of the external dynamics.
source: Formally, the task of distinguishing the true state of the world from uncertain, delayed measurements can be achieved by a Kalman filter, which continuously integrates new evidence with updated estimates of the current state, evolving according to a model of the external dynamics (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kalman filters.

claim: The Smith Predictor model readily accounted for the main features of human data, including the cursor amplitude response to perturbations.
source: The Smith Predictor model readily accounted for the main features of our human data, including the cursor amplitude response to perturbations (Figure 4A–E), and the low-pass filtering (Figure 4F–H) and phase delay (Figure 4I) of force responses.
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: The Smith Predictor model accounted for the low-pass filtering of force responses.
source: The Smith Predictor model readily accounted for the main features of our human data, including the cursor amplitude response to perturbations (Figure 4A–E), and the low-pass filtering (Figure 4F–H) and phase delay (Figure 4I) of force responses.
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: The Smith Predictor model accounted for the phase delay of force responses.
source: The Smith Predictor model readily accounted for the main features of our human data, including the cursor amplitude response to perturbations (Figure 4A–E), and the low-pass filtering (Figure 4F–H) and phase delay (Figure 4I) of force responses.
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: A predictive state estimator responding more quickly to low-frequency errors behaves like a feedback controller with a reduced loop delay.
source: Effectively, a predictive state estimator responding more quickly to low-frequency errors behaves like a feedback controller with a reduced loop delay.
evidence: This is an inference about the behavior of the model.

claim: The intrinsic delay time corresponding to each spectral peak was positively correlated with frequency (n = 11 spectral peaks, R = 0.78, p=0.0046).
source: Rather than being a constant, this intrinsic delay time was positively correlated with frequency (n = 11 spectral peaks, R = 0.78, p=0.0046) and matched well the frequency-dependent phase delay predicted by our model (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The intrinsic delay time matched well the frequency-dependent phase delay predicted by the model.
source: Rather than being a constant, this intrinsic delay time was positively correlated with frequency (n = 11 spectral peaks, R = 0.78, p=0.0046) and matched well the frequency-dependent phase delay predicted by our model (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental data and model predictions.

claim: Overall tracking performance matched well with subjects' actual performance across conditions.
source: Finally, overall tracking performance (as measured by the root mean squared positional error over time) matched well with subjects' actual performance across conditions in our second experiment (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: The Smith Predictor architecture requires accurate compensation for external delays within an internal feedback loop to generate stable tracking behavior.
source: However, in order to generate stable tracking behavior, the Smith Predictor architecture requires accurate compensation for external delays within an internal feedback loop.
evidence: This is a property of the Smith Predictor architecture.

claim: Feedback gains for different delay conditions became less similar as the trial progressed when assuming a simple feedback controller architecture.
source: Figure 5E shows the intrinsic gain that a simple feedback controller would need to explain the amplitude responses observed during 5 s sections of experimental data taken from the start, middle and end of each trial. While the general pattern was one of low-pass filtering, the intrinsic dynamics inferred for each delay condition diverged progressively through the trial.
evidence: This is an observation from analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Intrinsic feedback gains inferred using the Smith Predictor model became progressively more similar as the trial progressed.
source: Interestingly, intrinsic feedback gains inferred using the Smith Predictor model (Figure 5F) became progressively more similar as the trial progressed.
evidence: This is an observation from analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The adaptation process could be interpreted as the emergence of an appropriately-calibrated Smith Predictor with delay-independent intrinsic dynamics.
source: Therefore the adaptation process could parsimoniously be interpreted as the emergence of an appropriately-calibrated Smith Predictor with delay-independent intrinsic dynamics, as predicted by our optimal control model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on model predictions.

claim: The time-course of adaptation was associated with a reduction in both low-frequency phase delays and the average lag of the cursor behind the target.
source: The time-course of this adaptation (Figure 5G) was associated with a reduction in both low-frequency phase delays (Figure 5H) and the average lag of the cursor behind the target (Figure 5I), showing that subjects quickly learned to compensate for feedback delays within individual trials.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 5G-I.

claim: Subjects quickly learned to compensate for feedback delays within individual trials.
source: The time-course of this adaptation (Figure 5G) was associated with a reduction in both low-frequency phase delays (Figure 5H) and the average lag of the cursor behind the target (Figure 5I), showing that subjects quickly learned to compensate for feedback delays within individual trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the adaptation data.

claim: Movement intermittency was apparent as regular submovement peaks in the radial cursor velocity during the monkey tracking task.
source: Movement intermittency was apparent as regular submovement peaks in the radial cursor velocity.
evidence: This is an observation from the monkey experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: LFPs exhibited low-frequency oscillations during movement, with a variety of phase-shifts present on different channels.
source: Moreover, LFPs exhibited low-frequency oscillations during movement, with a variety of phase-shifts present on different channels.
evidence: This is an observation from the monkey LFP data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Principal component analysis yielded two orthogonal components of the cortical cycle.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) yielded two orthogonal components of the cortical cycle (Figure 6E), and the close coupling with submovements was revealed by overlaying the cursor velocity profile onto, in this case, the second principal component (PC) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method and results shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There was close coupling between cortical cycles and submovements.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) yielded two orthogonal components of the cortical cycle (Figure 6E), and the close coupling with submovements was revealed by overlaying the cursor velocity profile onto, in this case, the second principal component (PC) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In the absence of feedback delay, cursor velocity was dominated by a single spectral peak.
source: As with humans, in the absence of feedback delay the cursor velocity (after removing task-locked components, see Materials and methods) was dominated by a single spectral peak (Figure 7A,E; top red traces).
evidence: This is an observation from the monkey data shown in Figure 7A,E.

claim: A broad peak at approximately the same frequency as cursor velocity was observed in average LFP power spectra.
source: A broad peak at approximately the same frequency was also observed in average LFP power spectra (Figure 7B,F).
evidence: This is an observation from the monkey LFP data shown in Figure 7B,F.

claim: Coherence analysis confirmed consistent phase-coupling between LFPs and cursor velocity.
source: Additionally, we used coherence analysis to confirm consistent phase-coupling between LFPs and cursor velocity (Figure 7C,G).
evidence: This is a result from coherence analysis shown in Figure 7C,G.

claim: Imaginary coherence between pairs of LFPs revealed more clearly the LFP rhythmicity.
source: Finally, we calculated imaginary coherence spectra between pairs of LFPs (see Materials and methods). The imaginary component of coherence indicates frequencies at which there is consistent out-of-phase coupling in the LFP cross-spectrum. This effectively separates locally-varying oscillatory components from in-phase background signals (e.g. due to volume conduction from distant sources), and revealed more clearly the LFP rhythmicity (Figure 7D,H).
evidence: This is a result from imaginary coherence analysis shown in Figure 7D,H.

claim: With no feedback delay, all spectra contain a single peak at around 2-3 Hz.
source: Note that for no feedback delay, all spectra contain a single peak at around 2–3 Hz.
evidence: This is an observation from the monkey data shown in Figure 7.

claim: With increasing feedback delays, submovement peaks in monkeys exhibited a pattern similar to that seen with human subjects.
source: With increasing feedback delays, submovement peaks in monkeys (Figure 7A,E; lower traces) exhibited a pattern similar to that seen with human subjects.
evidence: This is a comparison between monkey and human data.

claim: The fundamental submovement frequency was reduced with increasing feedback delays in monkeys.
source: The fundamental frequency was reduced, while odd harmonics grew more pronounced as they came below about 4 Hz.
evidence: This is an observation from the monkey data shown in Figure 7A,E.

claim: Odd harmonics grew more pronounced as they came below about 4 Hz with increasing feedback delays in monkeys.
source: The fundamental frequency was reduced, while odd harmonics grew more pronounced as they came below about 4 Hz.
evidence: This is an observation from the monkey data shown in Figure 7A,E.

claim: Coherence spectra between cursor velocity and LFP revealed delay-dependent peaks at both fundamental and harmonic frequencies.
source: Moreover, coherence spectra between cursor velocity and LFP (Figure 7C,G) revealed delay-dependent peaks at both fundamental and harmonic frequencies.
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis shown in Figure 7C,G.

claim: The power spectrum of the LFP was unaffected by feedback delay, with a single broad peak in the delta band persisting throughout.
source: Surprisingly however, the power spectrum of the LFP (Figure 7B,F) was unaffected by feedback delay, with a single broad peak in the delta band persisting throughout.
evidence: This is an observation from the LFP power spectra shown in Figure 7B,F.

claim: Imaginary coherence spectra between pairs of LFPs were unchanged by feedback delay.
source: Moreover, imaginary coherence spectra between pairs of LFPs were also unchanged (Figure 7D,H).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaginary coherence analysis shown in Figure 7D,H.

claim: The results demonstrate a dissociation between delay-dependent submovements and delay-independent cortical dynamics.
source: These results are incompatible with the hypothesis that motor cortical oscillations drive movement intermittency directly, and instead demonstrate a dissociation between delay-dependent submovements and delay-independent cortical dynamics.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the monkey LFP and behavioral data.

claim: Submovement-triggered averages of LFPs exhibited multiphasic potentials around the time of movement.
source: Submovement-triggered averages (SmTAs) of LFPs exhibited multiphasic potentials around the time of movement, as well as a second feature following submovements with a latency that depended on extrinsic delay (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the submovement-triggered average analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Submovement-triggered averages of LFPs exhibited a second feature following submovements with a latency that depended on extrinsic delay.
source: Submovement-triggered averages (SmTAs) of LFPs exhibited multiphasic potentials around the time of movement, as well as a second feature following submovements with a latency that depended on extrinsic delay (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the submovement-triggered average analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: LFP oscillations around the time of submovements appeared largely unaffected by delay.
source: Importantly however, LFP oscillations around the time of submovements appeared largely unaffected by delay.
evidence: This is an observation from the submovement-triggered average analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: For all delay conditions, LFPs traced a single cycle with the same directional of rotation and comparable angular velocity.
source: For all delay conditions, LFPs traced a single cycle with the same directional of rotation and comparable angular velocity (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is an observation from the LFP-PC trajectory analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The period of LFP cycles (approx. 300 ms) matched the frequency of imaginary coherence between LFPs (approx. 3 Hz).
source: The period of these cycles (approx. 300 ms) matched the frequency of imaginary coherence between LFPs (approx. 3 Hz).
evidence: This is a comparison between two measures from the data.

claim: The precise frequency of submovements depended on extrinsic delays in visual feedback, while the constant frequency of associated LFP cycles revealed delay-independent intrinsic dynamics within motor cortex.
source: In other words, although the precise frequency of submovements depended on extrinsic delays in visual feedback, the constant frequency of associated LFP cycles revealed delay-independent intrinsic dynamics within motor cortex.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the monkey data.

claim: The resonant frequency of intrinsic dynamics matched the delay-independent filtering of feedback responses observed in human experiments.
source: Note also that the resonant frequency of these dynamics matched the delay-independent filtering of feedback responses observed in our human experiments.
evidence: This is a comparison between monkey and human data.

claim: The computational model could explain various observations including delay-dependent peaks/troughs in submovement-triggered averages reflecting extrinsic feedback delays.
source: Time-domain SmTAs of the simulated data also reproduced features of the experimental recordings, including delay-dependent peaks/troughs reflecting extrinsic feedback delays (Figure 8E–G).
evidence: This is a comparison between model simulations and experimental data.

claim: The coupling of simulated neural populations according to conserved intrinsic dynamics resulted in consistent LFP cycles around the time of movement.
source: Meanwhile, the coupling of simulated neural populations, according to conserved intrinsic dynamics, resulted in consistent LFP cycles around the time of movement (Figure 8H), and an imaginary cross-spectrum with a single delay-independent resonant peak (Figure 7L).
evidence: This is a description of model behavior shown in Figures 8H and 7L.

claim: K-complex events under ketamine sedation are associated with brief bursts of delta oscillation.
source: In particular, K-complex events under ketamine sedation (Figure 10A), thought to reflect transitions between down- and up-states of the cortex, are associated with brief bursts of delta oscillation (Figure 10B) (Amzica and Steriade, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation and shown in Figure 10A,B.

claim: The relative phases of multichannel LFPs aligned to K-complex events matches those seen during submovements.
source: The relative phases of multichannel LFPs aligned to these events matches those seen during submovements (Figure 10D,E).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 10D,E.

claim: When projected onto the PC plane, LFPs trace similar cycles during both K-complexes and submovements.
source: As a result, when projected onto the PC plane, LFPs trace similar cycles during both K-complexes (Figure 10C) and submovements (Figure 10F).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 10C,F.

claim: Transient excitation of the state estimator elicited an impulse response reflecting its intrinsic dynamics.
source: Effectively, transient excitation of the state estimator elicited an impulse response reflecting its intrinsic dynamics.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior during simulated K-complexes.

claim: The simulated LFPs generated a burst of delta-frequency oscillation around the K-complex which resembled submovement-related activity.
source: The simulated LFPs generated a burst of delta-frequency oscillation around the K-complex (Figure 10H) which resembled submovement-related activity (Figure 10J,K).
evidence: This is a comparison between simulated K-complex and submovement activity shown in Figures 10H,J,K.

claim: The computational model incorporating intrinsic dynamics of motor cortical networks could account for the conserved structure of low-frequency LFPs during movement and delta oscillations in sleep.
source: Thus it appears that our computational model, incorporating the intrinsic dynamics of motor cortical networks, could also account for the conserved structure of low-frequency LFPs during movement and delta oscillations in sleep.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Previous theories of intermittency have focused on either extrinsic or intrinsic explanations for the regularity of submovements.
source: Previous theories of intermittency have focused on either extrinsic or intrinsic explanations for the regularity of submovements, but little consensus has emerged over this fundamental feature of movement.
evidence: This is background knowledge about the state of the field.

claim: There is good evidence for a common low-frequency oscillatory structure to motor cortex activity across multiple behavioral states.
source: There is good evidence for a common low-frequency oscillatory structure to motor cortex activity across multiple behavioral states (Churchland et al., 2012; Hall et al., 2014; Russo et al., 2018) but also an influence of feedback delays on submovement timing (Miall, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Experimentally manipulating visual feedback with artificial time delays and spatial perturbations allowed dissociation of both contributions to submovement kinematics.
source: Experimentally manipulating visual feedback with artificial time delays and spatial perturbations allowed us to dissociate both contributions to submovement kinematics.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: Precise frequencies of submovement peaks were determined by delays in the extrinsic feedback loop.
source: We found that precise frequencies of submovement peaks were determined by delays in the extrinsic feedback loop, but that these were embedded within a delay-independent envelope reflecting intrinsic filtering of feedback corrections.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Submovement peaks were embedded within a delay-independent envelope reflecting intrinsic filtering of feedback corrections.
source: We found that precise frequencies of submovement peaks were determined by delays in the extrinsic feedback loop, but that these were embedded within a delay-independent envelope reflecting intrinsic filtering of feedback corrections.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Both delay-dependent feedback corrections and delay-independent cycles were observed in submovement-triggered averages of LFPs.
source: Both delay-dependent feedback corrections and delay-independent cycles were observed in submovement-triggered averages of LFPs.
evidence: This is a summary of the LFP findings.

claim: While coherence between LFPs and cursor movement exhibited delay-dependent spectral peaks, the imaginary coherence between multichannel LFPs revealed a consistent dynamical structure across behaviors.
source: Moreover, while coherence between LFPs and cursor movement exhibited delay-dependent spectral peaks, the imaginary coherence between multichannel LFPs revealed a consistent dynamical structure across behaviors.
evidence: This is a summary of the LFP coherence findings.

claim: The results could be explained by using a continuous feedback control model which incorporated optimal state estimation based on a second-order internal model of the external dynamics.
source: We were able to explain these apparently contradictory results by using a continuous feedback control model, which incorporated optimal state estimation based on a second-order internal model of the external dynamics.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling approach.

claim: Intermittency has been implemented in optimal feedback control models by explicitly including a refractory period between submovements.
source: Previously, intermittency has been implemented in optimal feedback control models by explicitly including a refractory period between submovements (Gawthrop et al., 2011; Sakaguchi et al., 2015), but theoretical justification for such an additions is lacking.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Theoretical justification for including a refractory period in optimal feedback control models is lacking.
source: Previously, intermittency has been implemented in optimal feedback control models by explicitly including a refractory period between submovements (Gawthrop et al., 2011; Sakaguchi et al., 2015), but theoretical justification for such an additions is lacking.
evidence: This is a critique of previous modeling approaches.

claim: In the model, submovements arose from constructive interference between motor errors and continuous, delayed feedback corrections.
source: In our model, submovements instead arose from constructive interference between motor errors and continuous, delayed feedback corrections.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: Optimal state estimation used a steady-state Kalman filter to separate process (motor) noise from measurement (sensory) noise.
source: Optimal state estimation used a steady-state Kalman filter to separate process (motor) noise from measurement (sensory) noise.
evidence: This is a description of the model component.

claim: 2-3 Hz intrinsic dynamics matched the frequency of the primary submovement peak under unperturbed external feedback conditions.
source: For example, it is notable that 2–3 Hz intrinsic dynamics matched the frequency of the primary submovement peak under unperturbed external feedback conditions, thus accentuating the fundamental submovement frequency around 2 Hz, while suppressing higher harmonics.
evidence: This is an observation about the relationship between model parameters and behavior.

claim: Force amplitude responses to cursor perturbations were uniformly less than unity.
source: One puzzling feature of our results was that force amplitude responses to cursor perturbations were uniformly less than unity, which initially appears suboptimal for rejecting even slow perturbations.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Sub-unity amplitude responses were observed when sinusoidal displacements were added to the target position.
source: However, sub-unity amplitude responses were also observed in separate experiments (not shown) when sinusoidal displacements were added to the target position.
evidence: This is a description of additional experimental observations.

claim: Subjects consistently undershot corrections to all but the lowest frequency perturbations even in the absence of any delay.
source: In this situation there was no discrepancy between vision and proprioception, yet subjects consistently undershot corrections to all but the lowest frequency perturbations (even in the absence of any delay).
evidence: This is an observation from additional experiments.

claim: Subjects avoided making corrections requiring large changes to the motor command.
source: An alternative explanation is that subjects avoided making corrections requiring large changes to the motor command.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the sub-unity amplitude responses.

claim: Proportional-integral (PI) control has been used in the past to model human movement.
source: This can be formalized by a cost function that is minimized by proportional-integral (PI) control, which has been used in the past to model human movement (Kleinman, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The trajectory variability observed in the isometric tracking task appeared more correlated with large changes in finger forces, rather than the absolute force magnitude.
source: However, the trajectory variability observed in our isometric tracking task appeared more correlated with large changes in finger forces, rather than the absolute force magnitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Derivative-dependent motor noise was evident as increased variability at high frequencies in the feedforward task.
source: Derivative-dependent motor noise was also evident as increased variability at high frequencies in our feedforward task (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the feedforward task data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Derivative-dependent motor noise provides an explanation for why the amplitude of submovements increases with target speed.
source: Since submovements result from constructive interference between tracking errors and feedback corrections, derivative-dependent motor noise also provides a counterintuitive, but necessary, explanation for why the amplitude of submovements increases with target speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PCA of multichannel LFPs in monkey motor cortex revealed two underlying components.
source: PCA of multichannel LFPs in monkey motor cortex revealed two underlying components, which we interpret as arising from distinct but coupled neural populations.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method and interpretation.

claim: The cyclical movement-related dynamics of LFP components resembled those described for M1 firing rates.
source: The cyclical movement-related dynamics of these components resembled those described for M1 firing rates (Churchland et al., 2012), which have previously been implicated in feedforward generation of movement.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work supported by citation.

claim: M1 firing rate dynamics have previously been implicated in feedforward generation of movement.
source: The cyclical movement-related dynamics of these components resembled those described for M1 firing rates (Churchland et al., 2012), which have previously been implicated in feedforward generation of movement.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It was proposed that preparatory activity first develops along 'output-null' dimensions before evolving via intrinsic dynamics into orthogonal 'output-potent' dimensions that drive muscles.
source: Specifically, it was proposed that preparatory activity first develops along 'output-null' dimensions of the neural state space before, at movement onset, evolving via intrinsic dynamics into orthogonal 'output-potent' dimensions that drive muscles (Churchland et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: The purely feedforward view cannot account for the isometric tracking data.
source: However, this purely feedforward view cannot account for our isometric tracking data, since manipulation of feedback delays dissociated delay-dependent submovements from delay-independent rotational dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The intrinsic dynamics implement a state estimator during continuous feedback control, driven by noise in motor and sensory signals.
source: Instead we interpret these intrinsic dynamics as implementing a state estimator during continuous feedback control, driven by noise in motor and sensory signals.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the findings.

claim: For discrete, fast movements to static targets, transient cursor-target discrepancies effectively provide impulse excitation to the state estimator, generating a rotational cycle in the neural space.
source: We suggest that for discrete, fast movements to static targets, transient cursor-target discrepancies effectively provide impulse excitation to the state estimator, generating a rotational cycle in the neural space.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how the model applies to different movement types.

claim: The state estimator account offers a natural explanation of why preparatory and movement-related activity lies along distinct state-space dimensions.
source: Note that this account also offers a natural explanation of why preparatory and movement-related activity lies along distinct state-space dimensions, since the static discrepancy present during preparation is encoded differently to the changing discrepancy that exists during movement.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the model.

claim: The lawful relationship between discrepancy and its derivative couples preparatory and movement dimensions within the state estimator and is evident as consistent rotational dynamics across different tasks and behavioral states.
source: At the same time, the lawful relationship between discrepancy and its derivative couples these dimensions within the state estimator and is evident as consistent rotational dynamics across different tasks and behavioral states.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the model.

claim: The computations involved in optimal tracking behaviors are likely distributed across multiple cortical areas including M1.
source: We suggest that the computations involved in optimal tracking behaviors are likely distributed across multiple cortical areas including (but not limited to) M1, with local circuitry reflecting multiple dynamical models of the various sensory and efference copy signals that must be integrated for accurate control.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the neural implementation of the model.

claim: An alternative explanation for consistent rotational dynamics has been proposed based on the behavior of recurrent neural networks trained to produce different feed-forward muscle patterns whilst minimizing 'tangling' between neural trajectories.
source: An alternative explanation for consistent rotational dynamics has recently been proposed by Russo et al. (2018), based on the behavior of recurrent neural networks trained to produce different feed-forward muscle patterns whilst minimizing 'tangling' between neural trajectories.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Both the tangling minimization and OFC approaches are motivated by the problem of maintaining accurate behavior in the presence of noise.
source: It is interesting to compare this with our OFC-based interpretation, since both are motivated by the problem of maintaining accurate behavior in the presence of noise.
evidence: This is a comparison between different theoretical approaches.

claim: Minimizing tangling leads to network architectures that are robust to intrinsic noise in individual neurons.
source: Minimizing tangling leads to network architectures that are robust to intrinsic noise in individual neurons, while OFC focusses on optimizing movements in the face of unreliable motor commands and noisy sensory signals.
evidence: This is a description of the tangling minimization approach.

claim: OFC focusses on optimizing movements in the face of unreliable motor commands and noisy sensory signals.
source: Minimizing tangling leads to network architectures that are robust to intrinsic noise in individual neurons, while OFC focusses on optimizing movements in the face of unreliable motor commands and noisy sensory signals.
evidence: This is a description of the OFC approach.

claim: Recurrent neural network approaches may learn implementations of computational architectures such as Kalman filters that minimize the influence of noise on behavior.
source: Given this conceptual link, it is perhaps unsurprising if recurrent neural network approaches learn implementations of computational architectures such as Kalman filters that minimize the influence of noise on behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the relationship between different modeling approaches.
